Vision-language-action policies · Robot manipulation · ManiSkill 3

Consolidate, then Gate:
Continual Learning of Manipulation Skills Without Forgetting

A pretrained vision-language-action policy learns manipulation tasks one after another. Re-expressing each skill in a small core of its action expert, then switching the other units off for that skill's instruction and freezing the core, keeps every earlier skill exactly as it was — without storing any old data.

Summary
  • Brain-inspired, instruction-dependent consolidation preserves manipulation skills during sequential learning. Under the small allocations explored here it gives a better trade-off between performance and task bookkeeping than PackNet; PackNet remains stronger at larger allocations.
  • A SmolVLA policy, seeing only a camera image, its joint angles and an instruction, learns PushCube and then StackCube in simulation. Plain fine-tuning keeps 1.0% of pushing; experience replay of 50 stored examples keeps 85.7%.
  • Consolidate-and-gate, with 5% of the network per task, keeps pushing at 93.3% (it was 93.3% before stacking was learned) and learns stacking to 51.0%. Its two-task average, 72.2%, matches replay of 500 stored examples (72.5%, 94 MiB of old data); the gate stores none.
  • A third task asks for the opposite stack in the same scene. With each method at its best configuration (the gate and PackNet at 5% of the network per task), the gated policy averages 66.6% over the three tasks, the highest of the continual learners: PackNet 61.4%, replay of 500 examples 59.8%, of 50 examples 47.8%, fine-tuning 22.1%. It still stacks red on green when asked 43.3% of the time (fine-tuning 0.0%, building the wrong stack 63.0% of the time; replay 3.0–28.3%).
  • PackNet reserves a share of every weight matrix per task instead of whole units. At a nominal 5% per task the gate keeps pushing at 93.3% against 85.3% and leads by 5.1 points after three tasks (seeds 0 / 1 / 2: +1.7 / +6.7 / +7.0). Across allocations (the gate ahead at 5%, 2.5% and 1% per task; PackNet at 10% and 25%) the gate degrades more slowly as each task's share shrinks (chart). Its task records take 8.6 kB instead of a 99.9 MB per-weight map.
  • The price is plasticity: frozen units make new skills harder to learn (stacking 51.0% vs 54.7% for fine-tuning in the two-task study).

Setup

A simulated Franka Panda arm in ManiSkill 3 learns tasks in sequence from motion-planner demonstrations. The policy is SmolVLA (0.45B parameters): its vision-language backbone stays frozen and its 100M-parameter flow-matching action expert is fine-tuned. Each task is learned once and never revisited; after each task every earlier task is tested again on new scenes.

Policy inputOne 256×256 camera image, 9 joint positions (7 arm, 2 fingers), the instruction text.
→
SmolVLAFrozen vision-language backbone; trainable action expert (flow matching, 10 denoising steps).
→
Output50 future actions (hand displacement x, y, z and gripper) at 20 Hz; the first 5 are executed, then the policy looks again.

No privileged information reaches the policy: object and target positions exist in the simulator and in the demonstration files, but only the image, the joint positions and the instruction are passed on. Success is read from the simulator only to score test episodes, which use scenes never seen in training.

Method: consolidate, gate, freeze

The action expert's computation is split into 752 unit groups: in each of its 16 layers, 15 attention heads and 32 blocks of 64 MLP units. Every task goes through the same cycle; after it is learned and before the next task starts:

1. Consolidate. A new core is chosen at random among the unit groups that no earlier task has reserved (5% of all groups, 38 of 752). The task is trained a little longer with every other group silenced except the earlier, frozen cores, so the skill is re-expressed in its own core plus the earlier ones: 2000 updates for pushing, which recovers from 12.0% to 93.3% with only its core active, and 24000 for stacking.

Share per task. Larger cores keep more of each skill but leave fewer free units for later tasks. The results use 5% per task; other shares, from 1% to 25%, are compared with PackNet below.

2. Gate by instruction. From then on, task k's instruction runs cores 1…k and switches every other group off. The instruction is a normal policy input, so the gate uses no extra information.

3. Freeze. While later tasks are learned, every weight on these gated paths is frozen. A new task uses the whole network, including the frozen cores, but only the groups no task has reserved can change.

Because the earlier task's gated computation only touches frozen weights, its behaviour is preserved by construction — the frozen weights change by exactly zero. The experiments therefore ask what this costs: how well new tasks are learned, and how much capacity each task consumes.

The idea follows context-dependent gating with synaptic stabilisation in the brain and in networks (Masse, Grant & Freedman, 2018); in machine-learning terms it is close to PackNet and HAT, applied to whole heads and MLP blocks and keyed by the language instruction.

Inside one layer

The action expert is a stack of 16 standard Transformer decoder layers; the weight names are those of the code, which SmolVLA inherits from its language model. A query head reaches the residual stream only through its own 64 columns of o_proj, and each block of 64 MLP neurons only through its own 64 columns of down_proj, so switching off a unit's 64 values removes exactly its contribution. The gate does this with hooks on the inputs of these two matrices. Key/value heads are shared by three query heads each, so they cannot be switched off alone; they are frozen with the core heads that read them.

The same 5% under PackNet

PackNet also reserves a share of the network for each task and uses the task's identity to choose what runs, but it reserves single weights: the 5% largest of every matrix. Under the pushing instruction our policy runs a few complete units of each layer and switches the rest off; PackNet runs every unit with about 5% of its weights. Both freeze a similar share after task 1 (7.3% and 6.6% of the action expert's weights), but what runs for each task takes 752 bits to describe for the gate and an owner for each of 99.9M weights for PackNet.

Results

We compare consolidate-and-gate with fine-tuning, EWC and experience replay (ER) storing 50 or 500 examples of each earlier task, and PackNet, the closest earlier method, which keeps a fixed share of every weight matrix per task (at the same 5% per task and the same retraining budget as our consolidation), plus two references that are not continual learners: joint training on all data at once, and separate checkpoints chosen by instruction. All methods start each stage from policies with the same number of updates on earlier tasks. Every number is the success rate on 100 test scenes per task, mean over 3 training seeds. After three tasks each method is reported at its best configuration, the same rule for every method.

Consolidate-and-gate and PackNet reserve part of the network for each task and are compared at a nominal 5% per task: the gate reserves 5% of the unit groups (38 of 752), PackNet 5% of every weight matrix. Counted in weights, including the key/value weights that the gate's attention heads share and the small state/action/time projections that both methods give the first task, the first task freezes 7.3% of the action expert with the gate and 6.6% with PackNet, the first two tasks 12.0% and 11.5% (mean of 3 seeds). After all three tasks

The third task asks for the reverse of the second in identical scenes, so the two stacking skills directly conflict and only the instruction tells them apart. Before it, the stacking skill is consolidated into a second core chosen outside the pushing core; the gated policy's third stage may then change only the 90% of the unit groups that neither earlier task uses (88% of the action expert's weights). Replay stores examples of each earlier task.

Performance against allocation

PackNet keeps a fixed share of every weight matrix per task, chosen by weight magnitude after the task is learned; the gate keeps whole heads and MLP blocks. Both were run at five allocations per task. Below 25% they share one recipe: 2000 consolidation (PackNet: retraining) updates for pushing, 24000 for stacking, and the state/action/time projections given whole to the first task. At 25% both use 500 updates for pushing and 24000 for stacking, and PackNet prunes the projections like every other matrix. After three tasks the gate is ahead at 5%, 2.5% and 1% per task and PackNet at 10% and 25% (gate vs PackNet, three-task average: 25%: 72.3% vs 75.4%; 10%: 67.6% vs 69.1%; 5%: 66.6% vs 61.4%; 2.5%: 58.9% vs 40.7%; 1%: 49.8% vs 29.7%). Pushing, scored right after its own stage, separates the methods most: as the share shrinks from 10% to 1% the gate keeps 95.7% → 79.7% and PackNet 96.0% → 27.3%. The nominal shares count unit groups for the gate and weights for PackNet, and at each share below 25% the gate freezes slightly more weights after task 1 (12.1% vs 11.5% at 10%, 7.3% vs 6.6% at 5%, 4.7% vs 4.1% at 2.5%, 2.9% vs 2.6% at 1%); the gate at 1% still keeps more pushing (79.7% with 2.9% of the weights frozen) than PackNet at 2.5% (36.7% with 4.1%).

Rollouts after the last task

Against PackNet at 5%

At 5% per task the gate is 5.1 points ahead after three tasks (66.6% vs 61.4%; seeds 0 / 1 / 2: +1.7 / +6.7 / +7.0), on pushing (93.3% vs 85.3%) and the newest task (63.0% vs 53.7%); red on green is level (43.3% vs 45.3%). Most of the gap is already there after the first task: the gate keeps pushing at 93.3% after consolidation, PackNet at 85.3%, and pruning the small projections too drops PackNet to 44.3%. Both ran on the same GPU type for every stage and seed.

Low task-bookkeeping overhead. The gate records which unit groups each task uses, 8.6 kB as stored here (one bit per unit group and task, 94 bytes, would do). PackNet records an owner for every weight: a 99.9 MB map as stored here, one byte per weight (one bit per weight and task is 12.5 MB).

Why it works

The analyses in this section use the reported configuration, 5% random cores, in the two-task study (test scenes unless stated).

Fine-tuning forgets within the first 50 updates

Success on the earlier and the new task while the second task is learned:

Both freezing and gating are needed

Pushing success after stage B, with the gate on or off when pushing is tested, for policies trained with or without freezing the core during stage B:

Gate onGate off
Core frozen during B93.3%0.3%
Core not frozen0.0%1.3%

Pushing success after stage B with 5% cores, 100 test scenes, mean of 3 seeds unless stated.

With the core frozen, switching the gate off when pushing is tested drops pushing from 93.3% to 0.3%: the units trained for stacking interfere. Without freezing, stage B rewrites the core: pushing is 0.0% with the gate on and 1.3% with it off.

Control: how many predicted actions to execute

The policy predicts 50 actions and executes the first 5 before looking again. Five gives the highest or near-highest success for every method. Executing more of each chunk without looking lowers stacking and loses most finished stacks by the end of the episode; executing fewer stacks less often but keeps more stacks. The gated policy's pushing stays at 92–95% up to 10 actions per chunk and falls to 80% and 73% at 25 and 50 (ER-50: 64% and 84%); fine-tuning pushes in at most 1% at any setting.

Next steps

Two preliminary results point to ways of improving the method.

Choosing the units of each core

Cores are chosen at random. A 5% core chosen by intervention instead, the unit groups whose silencing hurts pushing most, raises the two-task average from 72.2% to 75.0% (seeds 0/1/2: 72/74/71% and 72/77/76%), with pushing at 95.3% and stacking at 54.7% against 93.3% and 51.0%. Choosing each task's units by how much the task relies on them could improve the method further.

Two-task study, after stage B; 100 test scenes, mean ± SD over 3 seeds.

Making room when the network is full

Each task reserves a fixed share, so the network holds a fixed number of tasks. In a first test at 50% per task, the first two tasks fill the network: with nothing released, the third task cannot be learned (average over the three tasks 46.7% for the gate, 50.6% for PackNet, which is ahead at large allocations as above). Releasing half of each earlier share lets it in: the gate gives up its least important unit groups, keeps pushing at 93.3% and learns green on red to 42.0%; PackNet gives up its smallest weights and learns green on red to 58.3%, but its pushing falls to 42.3%. Both give up red on green, so a release that keeps the earlier skills, for example by consolidating each one into the units it keeps, is a next step.

Limitations

  • Capacity. Each task reserves a fixed share, so a fixed network holds a fixed number of tasks; a further task needs earlier tasks to give up part of theirs (next steps).
  • Larger allocations. PackNet is ahead at 10% and 25% per task: 69.1% vs 67.6% and 75.4% vs 72.3% after three tasks.
  • Scope. Simulation only, three tasks, one camera and 3 training seeds; each task is recognised by its exact instruction.

Reproduce

Everything runs from the repository on one GPU (an RTX 5090 trains two runs at once; the two-task study takes about 11 hours). Every reported run is one line in experiments/.

git clone https://github.com/DishengTang/continual_vla.git && cd continual_vla
export CVLA_ROOT=/path/to/large/disk
bash scripts/setup_env.sh && source scripts/env.sh
python scripts/download_assets.py && python scripts/replay_demos.py
MAX=2 bash experiments/run_jobs.sh experiments/01_main_study.jobs
python scripts/export_results.py --root $CVLA_RUNS/final --out results.json

Hardware and software

Runs were trained and scored on two GPU types. Every machine used ManiSkill 3.0.1, SAPIEN 3.0.3, Transformers 5.5.4 and PyTorch 2.11.0. Repeated evaluations of a checkpoint on one GPU type agree (exactly, or within one episode in a hundred), but the same checkpoint scored pushing 91% on the RTX 5090 and 85% on an RTX 4090 (validation scenes; 8 of 100 episodes ended differently). Differences of a few points between runs on different GPU types, such as the gate against ER-500 after two tasks, against joint training after three, and the two methods at 10% per task, are within this sensitivity.
